name: Production technique
controls: How the motion is actually made: the animation method and toolchain (keyframed vectors, hand-drawn frames, rigs, compositing, simulation, code and web runtimes, physical capture), which in turn shapes the look and feel of the result.
question: How should the motion be made, and should the technique show?
notes: Production technique is partly invisible (code-based versus keyframed can look identical) and partly a style in its own right (frame-by-frame boil, stop-motion stutter, rotoscoped wobble). Choose it here when the technique should be visible in the result or when it constrains the build. Rasa Director builds in HTML with GSAP through HyperFrames, rendered frame by frame from a paused, seekable timeline, so each option is classed by scope. Native: code-based animation, GSAP keyframe tweens of DOM/SVG/CSS properties (vector keyframe, shape-layer-style, motion-path via MotionPathPlugin), SVG animation, Canvas 2D drawn from timeline time, procedural and generative animation computed from time with seeded randomness, 2.5D compositing with CSS 3D transforms, and WebGL through the Three.js adapter. Supported through adapters: Lottie playback and CSS keyframes (HyperFrames runtime adapters exist, but Rasa Director's motion contract audits GSAP tweens, so GSAP is preferred for authored motion). Emulated: frame-by-frame and cel looks (stepped timing, boiling, image sequences), puppet rigging (nested transform hierarchies), physics and particle simulation (deterministic closed-form or pre-stepped), After Effects-style compositing (blend modes, masks, SVG filters), mixed media and stop-motion looks. Out of scope for a live build, but usable as pre-rendered footage or image sequences: true stop motion, rotoscoping, camera motion tracking, Rive runtime state machines, full 3D keyframe animation authored in DCC tools, and real-time interactive animation (a rendered video cannot be interactive). Industry usage: 'shape-layer animation' and 'After Effects-style compositing' are tool-derived terms from Adobe After Effects; 'procedural' and 'generative' overlap heavily (procedural: rule-driven motion toward an authored result; generative: a system producing varied, partly autonomous output).

options.what: Vector artwork animated by setting property values at key moments and letting software interpolate between them with easing curves.
options.looks: Crisp resolution-independent shapes and type; motion as smooth as its easing curves; the dominant look of contemporary motion graphics.
options.motion: Interpolated position, scale, rotation, opacity, color and path changes; character comes from easing and timing.
options.use: Almost all product motion, explainers, kinetic type, logo animation, UI animation.
options.vs: Frame-by-frame draws every frame; keyframe animation interpolates between a few. HyperFrames: native (GSAP tweens and timelines on SVG and DOM).
options.prompt: Animate vector artwork (inline SVG and DOM) with GSAP tweens on one paused timeline: key only the states that matter (start, accent, settle), let easing do the rest, and use a small set of named eases and durations for consistency. Avoid linear interpolation except for constant-speed motion.

options.what: Animation built from parametric shapes (rectangles, ellipses, paths) with animatable modifiers such as trim paths, repeaters, offsets and rounded corners.
options.looks: Clean geometric shapes, lines that draw and undraw, repeated radial patterns, morphing primitives; classic motion-graphics abstraction.
options.motion: Trim-path draw-ons, repeater bursts, corner-radius morphs, stroke-width swells, shape-to-shape morphs.
options.use: Logo stings, transitions, abstract accents, icon animation, explainer graphics.
options.conveys: Crisp craft, geometric energy, classic motion-graphics polish.
options.vs: Vector keyframe animation is the general method; shape-layer animation is the parametric-primitive toolkit (a term from After Effects). HyperFrames: native equivalent (SVG primitives with stroke-dashoffset for trim paths, cloned groups for repeaters, rx/ry for corner radius, MorphSVG-style path tweens).
options.prompt: Build graphics from SVG primitives and animate their parameters: trim-path draw-ons via stroke-dasharray/stroke-dashoffset (300-600ms, power2.inOut), repeaters as 6-12 cloned groups rotated or offset in constant steps with 30-60ms stagger, corner-radius and stroke-width tweens, and path morphs between shapes with matching point counts.

options.what: Objects travel along a defined curve, optionally rotating to follow its tangent.
options.looks: Elements flow along arcs, loops and routes; connections, journeys and orbits drawn by movement.
options.motion: Smooth curved travel with auto-orientation, speed controlled by easing along the path; paths often revealed or drawn in sync.
options.use: Flow diagrams, map routes, data traveling between nodes, cursors moving naturally, orbiting elements.
options.vs: Straight-line keyframes move in lines between points; motion paths define the curve explicitly. Text-on-path is type laid along a curve, not motion. HyperFrames: native (GSAP MotionPathPlugin with SVG paths).
options.prompt: Move objects along explicit SVG paths with GSAP MotionPathPlugin (path, align, autoRotate: true where orientation matters), easing along the path with power1.inOut. Draw the path simultaneously (stroke-dashoffset tied to the same progress) when the route itself is the message. Cursors use gentle arcs, never straight lines.

options.what: Keyframed animation of 3D objects, cameras and lights in a 3D package (Cinema 4D, Blender, Maya) or a real-time 3D engine.
options.looks: Lit, shaded 3D forms with real perspective, shadows and reflections; camera moves through space.
options.motion: Objects rotate, assemble, explode and orbit in 3D; cameras dolly and orbit; lighting animates.
options.use: Product hero films, 3D brand motion, device reveals, abstract 3D.
options.vs: 2.5D compositing moves flat layers in depth; 3D keyframe animation moves real geometry. HyperFrames: native for simple scenes via the Three.js adapter driven by the GSAP timeline; complex rigged or simulated 3D is out of scope and should come in as pre-rendered footage.
options.prompt: Animate 3D objects in a Three.js scene with GSAP tweens on object.position, rotation, scale and camera properties, all on the paused timeline (no requestAnimationFrame clock). Limit to primitives, extruded SVG shapes or loaded GLB models with a key light, fill and environment map. For anything more complex, render in a 3D package and composite as a video clip.

options.what: Every frame (or every second or third frame) drawn individually rather than interpolated.
options.looks: Organic, living lines that boil slightly; loose, expressive shapes and smears; unmistakably handmade.
options.motion: Timing on twos or threes (12 or 8 drawings per second), fluid morphing impossible with tweens, smears and squash drawn by hand.
options.use: Illustrated brand films, expressive transitions, character moments, music videos, doodle accents in product films.
options.vs: Cel animation is frame-by-frame with a specific ink-and-paint layering workflow; keyframe animation interpolates. HyperFrames: emulated (image or SVG sequences swapped with stepped timeline set() calls, boiled SVG filters, stepped eases); true hand-drawn frames must be supplied as assets.
options.prompt: Emulate frame-by-frame: time all motion on twos (steps at 12 fps) using GSAP ease 'steps(n)', swap between 2-3 slightly different drawings of each element (or boil lines with an feDisplacementMap whose seed steps every 2 frames), and use drawn smears on fast moves. If hand-drawn frames exist, play them as an image sequence with timeline-driven frame swaps.

options.what: Traditional animation in which drawn characters are inked and flat-painted on transparent cels layered over painted backgrounds.
options.looks: Clean ink outlines, flat color fills with hard-edged shadow shapes, rich painted backgrounds behind; classic animation-studio look.
options.motion: Frame-by-frame character motion on twos or threes over static or panning backgrounds; limited animation holds.
options.use: Anime-inspired and retro cartoon styles, character-led brand films, nostalgic campaigns.
options.conveys: Classic animation heritage, nostalgia, storytelling richness.
options.vs: Cel-shading in 3D is a render style mimicking the look; cel animation is the drawn process. Frame-by-frame is the broader method. HyperFrames: emulated (inked SVG with flat fills and hard shadow shapes, stepped timing, painted background layers).
options.prompt: Emulate cel animation: characters as inked SVG (2-3px dark outline, flat fills, one hard-edged shadow shape per form in a 20% darker tone) over a richer painted background layer; animate characters on twos (steps at 12 fps) while backgrounds pan smoothly; use holds with small secondary motion (blinks, hair) in the style of limited animation.

options.what: Tracing over live-action footage frame by frame, either to create animation with realistic motion or to cut out elements for compositing.
options.looks: Drawn or graphic figures moving with uncannily real human motion; outlines wobble slightly between frames.
options.motion: Realistic weight and timing from the source footage, rendered in a graphic style, often on twos.
options.use: Music videos, stylized brand films with people, documentary-illustration hybrids, masking footage.
options.conveys: Realism with artistry, dreamlike or documentary tone.
options.vs: Motion tracking follows points in footage without drawing; rotoscoping traces shapes. HyperFrames: out of scope as a live technique; bring in pre-traced sequences, or use footage with background removal (media tools) plus stylizing filters.
options.prompt: Treat rotoscoping as an asset: use pre-traced frame sequences (SVG or PNG, played by timeline-driven frame swaps on twos), or approximate it by running matted footage through a posterize and edge-detect SVG filter (feComponentTransfer discrete 3-4 steps plus a thin dark outline via feMorphology) with a slight per-2-frame boil.

options.what: Characters or objects built from separate parts connected in a hierarchy (and sometimes inverse kinematics) so they can be posed and animated like puppets.
options.looks: Cutout-style characters whose limbs rotate at joints; smooth, consistent poses; sometimes visibly jointed.
options.motion: Pose-to-pose animation, rotations at joints with overlap and follow-through, walk and gesture cycles.
options.use: Mascot-led explainers, character moments in product films, cutout-style brand animation.
options.vs: Frame-by-frame redraws the character; a rig re-poses the same parts. HyperFrames: emulated (nested SVG groups with transform-origin at joints, GSAP rotations with overlap); IK and mesh deformation are out of scope unless supplied via Lottie.
options.prompt: Rig the character as nested SVG groups (torso > upper arm > forearm > hand) with transform-origin set on each joint; animate pose-to-pose with GSAP rotations, offsetting child joints 40-80ms behind parents for overlap and follow-through, and settle with a small overshoot (back.out(1.2)). Keep a loopable idle (breathing scale 1-1.02, blink every 3-4s).

options.what: Building the frame from many stacked layers combined with blend modes, masks, mattes, adjustment effects and precomps.
options.looks: Rich layered frames: blended textures, masked footage, glows and light passes, graded color; the classic broadcast and motion-graphics finish.
options.motion: Layer-by-layer animation with masks revealing, mattes cutting, effects ramping; motion and effects interlocked.
options.use: Broadcast packages, title sequences, brand films, trailers, social ads.
options.vs: 2.5D compositing adds real depth to the layer stack; AE-style compositing can be flat. The term derives from Adobe After Effects. HyperFrames: emulated (CSS mix-blend-mode, mask-image, clip-path, SVG filters and nested compositions).
options.prompt: Composite in layers: build each scene as a stack of background, texture, subject, light and grade layers; combine with mix-blend-mode (multiply for shadows and textures, screen for light), reveal with mask-image and clip-path mattes, and apply effects via SVG filters. Organize repeated units as nested sub-compositions. Keep the layer count under about 12 per scene for render speed.

options.what: Flat layers positioned in 3D space and filmed with a virtual perspective camera to create parallax and depth.
options.looks: Flat artwork, photos or UI panels separated in depth; camera moves reveal parallax; layers never show their edges.
options.motion: Camera pushes, trucks and drifts through layers; depth-of-field shifts; layers rotate slightly toward camera.
options.use: Photo animation, documentary graphics, illustrated scenes, spatial UI product shots.
options.conveys: Cinematic depth and immersion from 2D assets.
options.vs: 2.5D in the depth dimension is the look; 2.5D compositing is the production method. 3D keyframe animation uses real geometry. HyperFrames: native (CSS perspective, transform-style: preserve-3d and translateZ).
options.prompt: Place flat layers in a perspective container (perspective 1200-1800px, transform-style: preserve-3d) at distinct translateZ depths, scaled by (perspective - z) / perspective to fill the frame; animate a camera wrapper (translateZ, translateX, small rotateY) on the timeline to create parallax. Blur far layers 2-6px for depth of field.

options.what: Analysing live-action footage to follow points, planes or the camera so graphics can be locked into the shot.
options.looks: Labels, UI and graphics that stick to moving objects, screens or surfaces in footage as if physically present.
options.motion: Graphics inherit the footage's motion (position, scale, rotation, perspective); callouts follow subjects; screens are replaced.
options.use: Tracked callouts in product videos, screen replacement, AR-style graphics, sports graphics.
options.vs: Rotoscoping traces shapes; tracking follows motion data. HyperFrames: out of scope as analysis; emulate by applying pre-computed tracking data (per-frame keyframes) to overlay elements, or use footage where the camera is locked.
options.prompt: Apply pre-computed tracking data: convert per-frame position, scale, rotation (and, for planar tracks, corner pins as a matrix3d) into a GSAP keyframe array on the overlay element, one key per frame, with ease 'none'. Without tracking data, compose graphics only over locked-off or very stable footage and keep overlays anchored to the frame, not the subject.

options.what: Combining techniques and source materials in one piece: footage, photography, illustration, 3D, scanned textures and type.
options.looks: Cutout photos with hand-drawn marks, vector UI over footage, paper textures behind 3D objects; visibly assembled.
options.motion: Each medium keeps its own motion character (stepped cutouts, smooth UI, real footage) in a single choreography.
options.use: Brand campaigns, editorial and culture pieces, social content, explainers that mix real and abstract.
options.vs: Collage is a visual style; mixed media is the production approach of combining techniques. HyperFrames: native (images, video clips, SVG, canvas and HTML layers compose freely), with hand-made assets supplied.
options.prompt: Combine at most three media deliberately (e.g. cutout photography, hand-drawn marker annotations, clean vector UI), giving each its own motion rule: cutouts move on twos with small rotations, drawn marks write on, UI tweens smoothly. Unify with a shared palette and one texture pass over everything.

options.what: Motion computed from rules, functions or expressions (sine waves, noise, offsets by index) rather than hand-set keyframes.
options.looks: Perfectly consistent waves, ripples, oscillations and cascades across many elements; systematic complexity.
options.motion: Values derived from time and index: sine oscillations, noise drift, distance-based delays, parametric patterns.
options.use: Pattern animation, grids and arrays, ambient backgrounds, data-driven motion, loops.
options.vs: Generative animation produces varied, partly autonomous output; procedural animation computes a defined result from rules. HyperFrames: native (compute from timeline time; GSAP stagger functions, utils.wrap, and custom onUpdate driven by the timeline's progress).
options.prompt: Drive motion procedurally from timeline time and element index: e.g. y = A * sin(2 pi (t / period) + index * phase) with A 8-24px, period 1.5-3s, phase 0.2-0.4 rad; delays from distance to a focal point (GSAP stagger: { from: 'center', grid, amount }). All values are pure functions of time so seeking is exact.

options.what: Motion computed by simulating forces: gravity, collisions, springs, friction and inertia.
options.looks: Objects falling, colliding, stacking and bouncing with believable weight; nothing looks hand-timed.
options.motion: Emergent: momentum, bounces with decreasing height, chain reactions, settling piles.
options.use: Playful product and brand motion, satisfying loops, physical metaphors (things falling into place), social content.
options.vs: Physics-based motion language imitates physics with eases and springs; physics simulation computes it. HyperFrames: emulated (closed-form projectile and damped-spring equations evaluated from timeline time, or a physics engine pre-stepped to baked keyframes); live engines ticking in real time are not seek-safe.
options.prompt: Emulate physics deterministically: compute falls with y = y0 + 0.5 g t^2 until contact, bounces with restitution 0.4-0.6 (each bounce 40-60% of the previous height) and springs with damped oscillation (x = A e^(-zeta w t) cos(w t)), all as functions of timeline time. For multi-body collisions, pre-step a physics engine offline and bake positions into per-frame keyframes.

options.what: Large numbers of small elements emitted and moved by forces (velocity, gravity, turbulence, attraction).
options.looks: Swarms, bursts, streams, dust fields and point clouds, sometimes assembling into shapes or logos.
options.motion: Emission, forces and lifetime-based fades; flocking, flowing, exploding and converging.
options.use: Celebrations, logo builds, AI and data metaphors, ambient backgrounds, transitions.
options.conveys: Energy, magic, abundance, data and intelligence.
options.vs: Particles (effects) is the visual treatment; particle simulation is the production method. HyperFrames: emulated (canvas 2D or Three.js points with a seeded generator and positions computed from timeline time); simulators with feedback (fluid-coupled particles) should be pre-rendered.
options.prompt: Implement particles on a canvas (or Three.js Points for thousands) with a seeded PRNG: each particle stores spawn time, origin, velocity, lifetime; draw every frame from the timeline's current time using closed-form motion (position = origin + v t + 0.5 g t^2, plus seeded sine turbulence). To assemble into a logo, interpolate each particle from its scattered position to a sampled target point with power3.inOut.

options.what: Animation produced by an algorithmic system that generates varied forms and motion, often from noise, rules or data, with the designer setting parameters rather than frames.
options.looks: Flow fields, organic growth, evolving patterns, data-driven forms; complex, often non-repeating output.
options.motion: Continuous evolution, emergence and variation; often loops seamlessly or runs indefinitely.
options.use: Generative brand identities, ambient backgrounds, event and installation visuals, AI themes.
options.conveys: Intelligence, life, endless variety, technological sophistication.
options.vs: Procedural animation computes a planned result from rules; generative animation lets a system produce variety within constraints. HyperFrames: native when the system is seeded and evaluated from timeline time (canvas, SVG or WebGL); systems depending on real-time feedback or unseeded randomness are not seek-safe.
options.prompt: Build the generative system on canvas or WebGL with a fixed seed: e.g. a flow field from seeded 3D simplex noise (x, y, time) advecting 500-3000 particles along traced lines, with palette colors only. Evaluate state from timeline time (pre-integrate trails per frame deterministically). Tune 2-3 parameters (noise scale, speed, density) to fit the brand rather than defaults.

options.what: Motion authored in code (JavaScript timelines, CSS, SVG, canvas, shaders) rather than in a timeline GUI.
options.looks: Can be anything; typically crisp, exact, systematic and data-driven, with pixel-perfect typography and UI.
options.motion: Tweens and timelines defined as code; reusable functions, data-driven sequences, exact timing.
options.use: Product motion with real UI, data visualization, templated social series, HyperFrames compositions.
options.conveys: Precision, scalability; the product's real interface can be used directly.
options.vs: Keyframe animation is a method; code-based is the medium it is authored in. HyperFrames: native, this is the build.
options.prompt: Author all motion as code on a single paused GSAP timeline registered for HyperFrames: reusable functions for repeated moves (enter, exit, emphasize), shared constants for eases and durations, real HTML/CSS for type and UI, and no time-based side effects outside the timeline.

options.what: Animating the geometry and attributes of SVG vector graphics: paths, strokes, fills, gradients, masks and filters.
options.looks: Crisp vectors at any scale; lines drawing on, shapes morphing, masks revealing, filter-based textures.
options.motion: Stroke draw-ons, path morphs, gradient stop shifts, mask and clip reveals, filter parameter tweens.
options.use: Icon and logo animation, illustrations, diagrams, line art, textures and filters.
options.vs: SMIL (SVG's built-in animation) is not seek-safe and should not be used; SVG animation here means tweening SVG attributes from the timeline. HyperFrames: native.
options.prompt: Animate inline SVG attributes with GSAP (attr: {}, stroke-dashoffset, fill, d via path morphing, gradient stop offsets, filter attributes such as feDisplacementMap scale or feTurbulence seed). Do not use SMIL <animate> or CSS @keyframes inside the SVG. Keep path point counts matched for morphs.

options.what: Animation declared in CSS with @keyframes, animation and transition properties, run by the browser.
options.looks: Typical web-UI motion: fades, slides, spins, loaders, hover transitions.
options.motion: Declarative loops and transitions with cubic-bezier timing; limited sequencing and no scrubbing on its own.
options.use: Website micro-interactions, loaders, simple loops.
options.vs: GSAP tweening CSS properties is code-based animation with full timeline control; CSS animation runs on the browser's own clock. HyperFrames: supported through its CSS-keyframes runtime adapter, but Rasa Director's motion contract audits GSAP tweens, so author motion as GSAP tweens of CSS properties and reserve @keyframes for trivial decorative loops, if any.
options.prompt: Express CSS-style motion as GSAP tweens of CSS properties on the paused timeline (transform, opacity, filter, clip-path, custom properties via @property), matching CSS cubic-bezier curves with CustomEase if needed. Do not use @keyframes or transition for anything the motion contract should see.

options.what: GPU-rendered 3D and shader effects in the browser via WebGL (usually through Three.js), enabling lighting, materials, post-processing and heavy effects.
options.looks: Real 3D objects, physically based materials, glass and refraction, fluid shader backgrounds, bloom and depth of field.
options.motion: 3D transforms, camera moves, shader uniforms (time, progress) animated for waves, distortions and transitions.
options.use: 3D product visuals, shader backgrounds, mesh gradients, image distortion transitions, particle clouds.
options.conveys: Technical sophistication, premium immersion, cutting-edge web craft.
options.vs: Canvas 2D draws flat pixels; WebGL renders on the GPU with shaders and 3D. HyperFrames: native through the Three.js adapter when every uniform and transform is driven by the paused timeline; heavy scenes slow rendering.
options.prompt: Use WebGL (Three.js) only where CSS/SVG cannot deliver: real 3D, refraction, shader distortions or thousands of particles. Drive every uniform (uTime, uProgress) and transform from the paused GSAP timeline and render on each timeline update, never from a requestAnimationFrame clock. Keep geometry and post-processing light.

options.what: Immediate-mode pixel drawing on an HTML canvas element, redrawn every frame.
options.looks: Anything drawable: particles, generative patterns, pixel effects, charts with thousands of points, image processing.
options.motion: Full redraw per frame from state; ideal for many small moving elements and pixel manipulation.
options.use: Particles, generative art, pixelation and dithering effects, dense data visualization.
options.vs: SVG is retained vector DOM (easier to tween individually, slower at scale); canvas is pixels redrawn from code (fast at scale, no per-element DOM). HyperFrames: native when drawn from timeline time.
options.prompt: Draw on a canvas sized at device resolution (2x for crispness) inside a function render(t) that is called from the timeline's onUpdate with the current time; all state derives from t and a fixed seed. Use canvas for elements numbering in the hundreds or more and for pixel effects; keep type and UI in HTML above it.

options.what: Vector animations exported from After Effects (via Bodymovin) or authoring tools as JSON and played back by a lightweight runtime.
options.looks: After Effects shape-layer animation (icons, illustrations, character loops) rendered crisply in SVG or canvas.
options.motion: Whatever was keyframed in the source tool, played back frame-accurately; no runtime logic.
options.use: Animated icons, illustrations and mascots in apps and websites, onboarding animations.
options.vs: Rive adds interactive state machines and its own editor; Lottie is linear playback of AE animation. HyperFrames: supported through the Lottie runtime adapter (seekable, frame-accurate); author new motion in GSAP unless a Lottie asset already exists.
options.prompt: Play existing Lottie assets through the HyperFrames Lottie adapter, with playback seeked from the timeline (goToAndStop by frame) rather than autoplay. Match the Lottie's colors to the palette (edit the JSON color arrays if needed) and scale it to the grid. Do not recreate a Lottie that already exists; do not author new complex motion as Lottie.

options.what: An interactive animation tool and runtime that plays vector animations controlled by state machines, bones and inputs in real time.
options.looks: Crisp vector characters and UI with smooth rigged motion, meshes and blend states; interactive in apps.
options.motion: State-machine-driven blends between animations, responsive to input (hover, click, data).
options.use: Interactive app mascots, product UI micro-interactions, game UI, interactive onboarding.
options.conveys: Interactive delight, responsiveness, modern app polish.
options.vs: Lottie is linear playback; Rive is interactive and state-based. HyperFrames: out of scope (no Rive adapter); emulate the look with rigged SVG and GSAP, or export the Rive animation to video and composite it.
options.prompt: Do not embed the Rive runtime. Reproduce Rive-style motion with rigged SVG (nested groups with joint transform-origins) and GSAP, playing the intended state transitions as a scripted sequence (idle, hover, press, success) with blended overlaps of 100-200ms; or composite an exported Rive video clip.

options.what: Animation computed and rendered live as it plays (game engines, interactive web, live visuals), responding to input or data.
options.looks: Game-engine 3D, responsive UI, audio-reactive visuals; can vary each time it runs.
options.motion: Driven by a live clock and inputs rather than a fixed timeline; physics and interaction evaluated per frame.
options.use: Interactive sites, installations, live event visuals, games, VJ sets.
options.vs: Rendered video is fixed; real-time is live and interactive. HyperFrames: out of scope as behavior (renders are deterministic frames from a seekable timeline); emulate the look with seeded, time-driven systems.
search: real time animation unreal engine motion design
options.prompt: Emulate real-time visuals as deterministic, timeline-driven systems: replace live inputs with scripted input curves (cursor paths, data series, audio envelopes pre-analysed into keyframes) and replace live clocks with the timeline's time, so the render looks live but is identical every time.

options.what: Physical objects photographed one frame at a time, moved slightly between each shot.
options.looks: Real materials (clay, paper, objects) with real light; slight jitter and lighting flicker between frames; tactile charm.
options.motion: Stepped at 8-15 fps, small inconsistencies frame to frame, no motion blur, objects hop rather than glide.
options.use: Craft and food brands, playful campaigns, social content, handmade explainers.
options.vs: Stop-motion-like motion language imitates the stepped timing with digital assets; stop motion is photographed. HyperFrames: out of scope as capture; use photographed sequences as assets, or emulate with stepped timing (steps at 12 fps), 1-2px per-frame position jitter and slight exposure flicker.
options.prompt: Emulate stop motion: time every move on steps at 12 fps (ease 'steps(n)'), add a 1-2px position and 0.3-degree rotation jitter per step from a fixed seed, flicker overall brightness by plus or minus 2% per step, avoid all motion blur and smooth eases, and use photographed or material-textured assets (clay, paper, objects). Photographed frame sequences play via timeline-driven frame swaps.
